hints: Start by counting electron pairs around nitrogen in $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{NH}_4^+$, remembering lone pairs change the shape.
$\text{NH}_3$ has 3 bond pairs plus 1 lone pair, while $\text{NH}_4^+$ has 4 bond pairs and no lone pair on nitrogen.
Think about whether a single N-H bond can ever be a pi bond, and whether a dative bond changes the bond type.
walkthrough:
**Draw the electron pairs for ammonia**

Ammonia is $\text{NH}_3$. Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons, it forms 3 bonds to H and keeps 1 lone pair.

So: 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 4 pairs total, pyramidal shape.

**Draw the electron pairs for ammonium**

Ammonium is $\text{NH}_4^+$. The lone pair on $\text{NH}_3$ accepts $\text{H}^+$, forming a fourth N-H bond.

So: 4 bond pairs + 0 lone pairs = regular tetrahedral shape.

**Decide sigma or pi**

All N-H bonds are single bonds. Every single bond is a $\sigma$ bond formed by direct head-on overlap.

$$\text{single bond} = 1 \times \sigma \text{ bond, no } \pi$$

**Put the row together**

Ammonia: pyramidal, $\sigma$ only. Ammonium: regular tetrahedral, $\sigma$ only, even though one bond is dative covalent.

That combination matches only one row.

options.A: Correct. $\text{NH}_3$ is pyramidal due to the lone pair repelling the 3 bond pairs, and $\text{NH}_4^+$ is regular tetrahedral with 4 equal bond pairs. Both contain only single N-H $\sigma$ bonds.
options.B: Shapes are right but bond type for ammonium is wrong. Students sometimes think the dative covalent bond is different or is a $\pi$ bond. It is still a single $\sigma$ bond once formed, just different in origin.
options.C: Shapes are swapped. A common slip is to forget the lone pair on ammonia and call it tetrahedral, and to forget that adding $\text{H}^+$ removes the lone pair to give tetrahedral ammonium, not pyramidal.
options.D: Both shapes are swapped and ammonia is given as $\pi$. Single N-H bonds can never be $\pi$ bonds. $\pi$ bonds only occur in double and triple bonds from sideways overlap.
